```{r}
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
library(broom)
library(gt)

# Site tokens (see custom.scss / DESIGN_SYSTEM.md)
sage  <- "#5C715E"  # $accent
sage2 <- "#8FAF9E"  # $accent2
sage3 <- "#A7C7B5"  # $accent3
ink   <- "#2F3E46"  # $body-color
hot   <- "#B5483B"  # "look here" highlight
amber <- "#E8A33D"
grp_cols <- c(sage2, amber)

theme_deck <- function(base_size = 22) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      axis.title = element_text(color = ink),
      axis.text = element_text(color = ink),
      plot.title = element_text(color = ink, face = "bold"),
      legend.text = element_text(color = ink),
      legend.position = "none"
    )
}

# Formatting helpers so every number on a slide comes from the data.
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
fp <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste("=", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p))))

# Pooled independent-samples t-test summary (first factor level minus second).
ind_stats <- function(y, g) {
  g <- factor(g); lv <- levels(g)
  a <- y[g == lv[1]]; b <- y[g == lv[2]]
  tt <- t.test(a, b, var.equal = TRUE)
  sp <- sqrt(((length(a) - 1) * var(a) + (length(b) - 1) * var(b)) /
               (length(a) + length(b) - 2))
  list(lv = lv, n1 = length(a), n2 = length(b), m1 = mean(a), m2 = mean(b),
       s1 = sd(a), s2 = sd(b), sp = sp, diff = mean(a) - mean(b),
       t = unname(tt$statistic), df = unname(tt$parameter), p = tt$p.value,
       ci = tt$conf.int, d = (mean(a) - mean(b)) / sp)
}
apa_t <- function(r) sprintf("t(%d) = %s, p %s", r$df, f2(r$t), fp(r$p))

# ---- Example datasets -------------------------------------------------
# Coffee vs. decaf happiness (built to have exactly these means and SDs)
set.seed(11)
exact <- function(n, m, sd) m + sd * scale(rnorm(n))[, 1]
coffee <- tibble(
  grp = factor(rep(c("Experimental", "Control"), each = 10),
               levels = c("Experimental", "Control")),
  happy = c(exact(10, 8, 1), exact(10, 6, 1))
)
cf <- ind_stats(coffee$happy, coffee$grp)

# Chocolate and concentration (0-20 scale)
set.seed(42)
choco <- data.frame(
  concentration = c(rnorm(25, 15, 2), rnorm(25, 13.5, 2)),
  group = factor(rep(c("chocolate", "no_chocolate"), each = 25),
                 levels = c("chocolate", "no_chocolate"))
)
ch <- ind_stats(choco$concentration, choco$group)

# Music and studying (0-10 quiz)
set.seed(99)
music <- data.frame(
  quiz_score = c(rnorm(20, 8, 1), rnorm(20, 7, 1.2)) |> pmin(10),
  group = factor(rep(c("music", "silence"), each = 20),
                 levels = c("music", "silence"))
)
mu_ <- ind_stats(music$quiz_score, music$group)

# Phone use and sleep quality (1-10 scale)
set.seed(77)
sleep <- data.frame(
  sleep_quality = c(rnorm(40, 6.8, 1), rnorm(40, 7.4, 0.9)),
  group = factor(rep(c("phone", "no_phone"), each = 40),
                 levels = c("no_phone", "phone"))
)
sl <- ind_stats(sleep$sleep_quality, sleep$group)

# Practice datasets
set.seed(103)
ex_3 <- tibble(
  Group = factor(rep(c("Caffeine", "Placebo"), each = 20),
                 levels = c("Caffeine", "Placebo")),
  Alertness = c(rnorm(20, mean = 75, sd = 8), rnorm(20, mean = 68, sd = 8))
)
set.seed(104)
ex_4 <- tibble(
  Format = factor(rep(c("Online", "InPerson"), each = 25),
                  levels = c("Online", "InPerson")),
  Exam_Score = c(rnorm(25, mean = 82, sd = 5), rnorm(25, mean = 79, sd = 6))
)
e3 <- ind_stats(ex_3$Alertness, ex_3$Group)
e4 <- ind_stats(ex_4$Exam_Score, ex_4$Format)

# A reusable results plot for each worked example
group_plot <- function(d, x, y, ylab, title, kind = "box") {
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(.data[[x]], .data[[y]], fill = .data[[x]]))
  p <- switch(kind,
    box = p + geom_boxplot(alpha = .6, outlier.shape = NA),
    violin = p + geom_violin(alpha = .5, trim = FALSE),
    bar = p + stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "col", width = .5, alpha = .8))
  p +
    geom_jitter(width = .12, alpha = .5, size = 2, color = ink) +
    stat_summary(fun.data = mean_se, geom = "errorbar", width = .2, color = ink) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = grp_cols) +
    labs(title = title, y = ylab, x = NULL) +
    theme_deck(20)
}

# Results table for a worked example
results_tbl <- function(r) {
  tibble(
    Difference = r$diff, t = r$t, df = r$df,
    p = ifelse(r$p < .001, "<.001", sprintf("%.3f", r$p)),
    `CI[ll,uu]` = paste0("[", f2(r$ci[1]), ", ", f2(r$ci[2]), "]"),
    d = r$d
  ) |>
    gt() |>
    fmt_number(columns = c(Difference, t, d), decimals = 2) |>
    fmt_number(columns = df, decimals = 0) |>
    opt_row_striping() |>
    tab_options(table.font.size = 22, table.width = pct(100)) |>
    tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
              locations = cells_column_labels())
}
```

## From Paired to Independent Samples

Last time, we compared **two related means**: the *same participants* measured twice (e.g., stress before vs. after a mindfulness program).

Now, we'll compare **two unrelated means**: *different participants* in each group.

| Paired t-test                          | Independent t-test             |
|----------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Same people                            | Different people               |
| Within-subjects                        | Between-subjects               |
| Reduces error (individual differences) | Must estimate error separately |

## From Paired to Independent Samples

### Visual comparison

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.8
library(patchwork)
set.seed(5)
paired <- tibble(
  condition = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Post"), each = 10), levels = c("Pre", "Post")),
  id = rep(1:10, 2)
) |> mutate(score = c(rnorm(10, 70, 5)) |> (\(x) c(x, x + 5 + rnorm(10, 0, 2)))())
independent <- tibble(
  group = rep(c("Control", "Experimental"), each = 10),
  score = c(rnorm(10, 70, 5), rnorm(10, 75, 5))
)

p1 <- ggplot(paired, aes(condition, score, group = id)) +
  geom_line(color = sage3, linewidth = .9) +
  geom_point(color = sage, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Paired: same people", y = "Score", x = NULL) +
  theme_deck(20)

p2 <- ggplot(independent, aes(group, score, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = .1, color = ink, alpha = .6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = grp_cols) +
  labs(title = "Independent: different people", y = "Score", x = NULL) +
  theme_deck(20)

p1 + p2
```

## Sampling Theory (Recap)

### Comparing two unrelated groups

- Sampling theory lets us test two unrelated groups.

- Under $H_0$ the **difference** between group means is centered on 0. Under $H_A$ it is centered somewhere else.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.8
rec_dat <- tibble(
  x = rep(seq(-5, 6, length.out = 400), 2),
  y = c(dnorm(seq(-5, 6, length.out = 400), 0, 1),
        dnorm(seq(-5, 6, length.out = 400), 2, 1)),
  hypothesis = factor(rep(c("Null hypothesis", "Alternative hypothesis"), each = 400),
                      levels = c("Null hypothesis", "Alternative hypothesis"))
)
rec_plot <- ggplot(rec_dat, aes(x, y, color = hypothesis, linetype = hypothesis)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(sage, ink)) +
  labs(x = "Difference between the group means (in standard errors)", y = NULL,
       color = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_deck(20) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
rec_plot
```

## Sampling Theory (Recap)

### A difference near 0 looks like the null

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.8
rec_plot + geom_vline(xintercept = -.8, color = hot, linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("text", x = -.8, y = .42, label = "observed", color = hot, hjust = 1.1, size = 6)
```

- An observed difference like this is easy to produce when $H_0$ is true.

## Sampling Theory (Recap)

### A difference beyond the critical value does not

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.8
rec_plot +
  geom_vline(xintercept = qnorm(.95), color = ink, linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = qnorm(.95), y = .42, label = "critical value",
           color = ink, hjust = -.1, size = 6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2.2, color = hot, linewidth = 1.3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.2, y = .3, label = "observed", color = hot, hjust = -.15, size = 6)
```

- Beyond the critical value, the observed difference would be very unusual under $H_0$, so we **reject** it.

## Inferential Statistics

### Applied to independent groups

- Our goal is still to test whether a difference is likely due to chance.

- With independent samples, chance variation now includes **differences between individuals** in *both* groups.

## Group Variance

### Within and between

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
To compare the means we need to know:

- **Between-group variance:** how much the answers from the **experimental** group differ from the **control** group.

- **Within-group variance:** how much the **answers of all participants** differ from one another.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.4
set.seed(3)
gv <- tibble(
  treatment = factor(rep(c("Experimental", "Control"), each = 30),
                     levels = c("Experimental", "Control")),
  score = c(rnorm(30, 30, 4), rnorm(30, 38, 4))
)
ggplot(gv, aes(treatment, score, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = .35, width = .8, color = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = .1, alpha = .5, size = 2, color = ink) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 5, color = hot) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = grp_cols) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Score", subtitle = "red dot = group mean") +
  theme_deck(20)
```
:::
:::::

## Independent-Samples t-Test Overview

Used when we compare **two different groups** on a continuous outcome.

:::::: badge-row
::: content-badge
[local_cafe]{.material-icons}

#### Coffee vs. decaf

Happiness scores
:::

::: content-badge
[headphones]{.material-icons}

#### Music vs. silence

Study performance
:::

::: content-badge
[smartphone]{.material-icons}

#### Phone vs. no phone

Sleep quality before bed
:::
::::::

- **Goal:** is the mean difference between groups larger than what we'd expect by chance?

## Independent-Samples t-Test

### Example

> The experimental group drinks caffeinated coffee. The control group drinks decaf. I ask both groups to complete a survey to measure their happiness on a scale of `1` to `10`.

- The experimental group has a mean happiness score of `8`.

- The control group has a mean happiness score of `6`.

::: fragment
Is the group that drank coffee significantly happier than the control group?
:::

## Formulas

### Theoretical and computational

Inferential statistics have both **theoretical** and **computational** formulas:

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Theoretical

The formula if we actually knew the population parameters ($\sigma$).
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
## Computational

The formula for estimating the test statistic based solely on sample data.
:::
:::
:::::

## Theoretical Formula

### If we knew the population standard deviation

$$z = \frac{\color{red}{\bar{x}_1} - \color{orange}{\bar{x}_2}}{\color{grey}{\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}}}$$

- [Sample mean, group 1]{style="color:red"}

- [Sample mean, group 2]{style="color:orange"}

- [Standard error of the difference]{style="color:grey"}, using the population $\sigma$ (assumed equal in both groups)

## Computational Formula

### Estimating from the samples (pooled t-test)

$$t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\color{darkblue}{s_p^2}\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}} \qquad s_p^2 = \frac{(n_1 - 1)s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)s_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}$$

- [$s_p^2$ = pooled variance]{style="color: darkblue"}, a weighted average of the two group variances.

- $df = n_1 + n_2 - 2$

## Computational Formula

### When the variances are not equal (Welch's t-test)

$$t = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}}$$

- No pooling: each group's variance keeps its own weight, and df is adjusted (it is usually not a whole number).

- This is what `t.test()` does **by default** in R. Adding `var.equal = TRUE` gives the pooled version above.

## Coffee Example

### Manual

::: callout-tip
## Pooled variance and standard error

$s_p^2 = \dfrac{(10-1)(1)^2 + (10-1)(1)^2}{10 + 10 - 2} = `r f2(cf$sp^2)`$ and $SE = \sqrt{`r f2(cf$sp^2)`\left(\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10}\right)} = `r f2(sqrt(cf$sp^2 * (1/cf$n1 + 1/cf$n2)))`$
:::

::: callout-tip
## Compute t

$t = \dfrac{8 - 6}{`r f2(sqrt(cf$sp^2 * (1/cf$n1 + 1/cf$n2)))`} = `r f2(cf$t)`$
:::

::: callout-tip
## Decide

$df = 10 + 10 - 2 = `r cf$df`$. At $\alpha = .05$ (two-tailed), $t_{critical} = \pm `r f3(qt(.975, cf$df))`$. Since $`r f2(cf$t)` > `r f3(qt(.975, cf$df))`$, we **reject** $H_0$.
:::

## Coffee Example

### Data overview

```{r}
#| echo: false
t.test(happy ~ grp, data = coffee, var.equal = TRUE) |>
  tidy() |>
  rename(mdiff = estimate, t = statistic, Experimental = estimate1,
         Control = estimate2, df = parameter) |>
  mutate(`CI[ll,uu]` = paste0("[", round(conf.low, 2), ", ", round(conf.high, 2), "]"),
         p = ifelse(p.value < .001, "<.001", sprintf("%.3f", p.value))) |>
  select(mdiff, t, df, p, Experimental, Control, `CI[ll,uu]`) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(mdiff, t, Experimental, Control), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = df, decimals = 0) |>
  opt_row_striping() |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = 30, table.width = pct(80)) |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_column_labels())
```

- `mdiff` is the experimental mean minus the control mean ($8 - 6 = 2$). The factor levels set the order, so put the group you want **first** to get a positive difference.

## Independent-Samples t-Test

### Assumptions

::: callout-important
## Assumptions

1.  **DV is continuous** (interval or ratio scale).
2.  **Observations are independent**, and the data are randomly sampled. Each person appears in only one group.
3.  **Normality:** each group's distribution is approximately normal (or the groups are large enough for the CLT).
4.  **Homogeneity of variance:** variances are similar across groups (tested with **Levene's Test**).
:::

## Interpreting Levene's Test

- Levene's Test tells us whether the assumption of equal variances holds.

  - If $p > .05$ → use the **top row** ("Equal variances assumed")

  - If $p < .05$ → use the **bottom row** ("Equal variances not assumed")

- Normality: each group's distribution should be approximately normal.

## Independent-Samples t-Test

### Homogeneity of variance

![](images/spiderman.png){style="border-radius: 20px;" width="300"}

::: fragment
If **Levene's Test** is significant, use the t value from the second row and its corresponding significance.
:::

- t is the test statistic.

- Sig. (2-tailed) is the p-value.

## Why Do We Care?

We need **Levene's Test** because if the variance of the experimental group is not equal to the variance of the control group, pooling the two variances is not appropriate. We switch to the unpooled (**Welch**) version of the test, which does not assume equal variances.

- A significant Levene's Test means a significant difference in the variances.

## Let's Apply It

### Three independent designs

We'll test three common between-subjects designs:

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Design

> 50 undergraduate students from XYZ University were randomly assigned to one of two groups. One group received a small piece of chocolate (70% dark cocoa) to consume before completing a 10-minute concentration task. The other group received no chocolate. The task measured sustained attention and was scored on a 0-20 scale.

- **IV:** chocolate (yes vs. no)

- **DV:** concentration task score

- **Design:** between-subjects, randomized

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Hypotheses

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Null hypothesis $H_0$

Concentration is the same with and without chocolate.

$\mu_\text{chocolate} = \mu_\text{no chocolate}$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
## Alternative hypothesis $H_A$

Concentration differs between the groups.

$\mu_\text{chocolate} \neq \mu_\text{no chocolate}$
:::
:::
:::::

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Data and results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.2
group_plot(choco, "group", "concentration", "Concentration score",
           "Chocolate and concentration")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
results_tbl(ch)
```

Chocolate: $M = `r f2(ch$m1)`$, $SD = `r f2(ch$s1)`$. No chocolate: $M = `r f2(ch$m2)`$, $SD = `r f2(ch$s2)`$.
:::
:::::

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Check the assumption

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
levene.R

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
library(car)

# Equal variances? (H0: the variances are equal)
leveneTest(concentration ~ group, data = choco)
```
:::

- Levene's $p > .05$, so equal variances are reasonable and the pooled test is appropriate.

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Run the test

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
chocolate.R

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
# Pooled (equal variances) t-test
t.test(concentration ~ group, data = choco, var.equal = TRUE)
```
:::

## Does chocolate improve concentration?

### Decision, effect size, and report

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Decide

$t(`r ch$df`) = `r f2(ch$t)`$, $p$ `r fp(ch$p)`. Since $p < .05$, we **reject** $H_0$.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Effect size

$d = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p} = \dfrac{`r f2(ch$diff)`}{`r f2(ch$sp)`} = `r f2(ch$d)`$ (a **large** effect)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
> An independent-samples t-test showed that students who ate chocolate (*M* = `r f2(ch$m1)`, *SD* = `r f2(ch$s1)`) scored significantly higher on the concentration task than students who did not (*M* = `r f2(ch$m2)`, *SD* = `r f2(ch$s2)`), [*`r apa_t(ch)`*]{.hl}, 95% CI [`r f2(ch$ci[1])`, `r f2(ch$ci[2])`], *d* = `r f2(ch$d)`.
:::
:::::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Design

> **Design Summary**\
> 40 students participated in a study examining how background music affects studying. Participants were randomly assigned to study a short academic text under one of two conditions: instrumental music or silence. After 15 minutes of study time, they completed a 10-item multiple-choice quiz.

- **IV:** study condition (instrumental music vs. silence)

- **DV:** quiz performance (number of correct answers out of 10)

- **Design:** between-subjects, randomized

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Hypotheses

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Null hypothesis $H_0$

Quiz performance is the same with music and in silence.

$\mu_\text{music} = \mu_\text{silence}$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
## Alternative hypothesis $H_A$

Quiz performance differs between the conditions.

$\mu_\text{music} \neq \mu_\text{silence}$
:::
:::
:::::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Data and results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.2
group_plot(music, "group", "quiz_score", "Quiz score (out of 10)",
           "Music and study performance", kind = "violin")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
results_tbl(mu_)
```

Music: $M = `r f2(mu_$m1)`$, $SD = `r f2(mu_$s1)`$. Silence: $M = `r f2(mu_$m2)`$, $SD = `r f2(mu_$s2)`$.
:::
:::::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Run the test

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
music.R

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
t.test(quiz_score ~ group, data = music, var.equal = TRUE)
```
:::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Decision, effect size, and report

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Decide

$t(`r mu_$df`) = `r f2(mu_$t)`$, $p$ `r fp(mu_$p)`. Since $p > .05$, we **fail to reject** $H_0$.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Effect size

$d = \dfrac{`r f2(mu_$diff)`}{`r f2(mu_$sp)`} = `r f2(mu_$d)`$ (a **medium** effect)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
> An independent-samples t-test showed that students who studied with music (*M* = `r f2(mu_$m1)`, *SD* = `r f2(mu_$s1)`) did not differ significantly on the quiz from students who studied in silence (*M* = `r f2(mu_$m2)`, *SD* = `r f2(mu_$s2)`), [*`r apa_t(mu_)`*]{.hl}, 95% CI [`r f2(mu_$ci[1])`, `r f2(mu_$ci[2])`], *d* = `r f2(mu_$d)`.
:::
:::::

## Does instrumental music improve studying?

### Reading a non-significant result

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
A medium effect that is *not* significant is a hint that the study may have been too small to detect it. (If we had predicted a *direction* before collecting data, the one-tailed $p$ would be about `r f3(mu_$p / 2)`. But the direction has to be chosen **before** you see the result.)
:::

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Design

> **Design Summary**\
> 80 students were randomly assigned to avoid phone use for 30 minutes before bed or to use their phones as normal. The next morning, all students rated their sleep quality on a 1-10 scale.

- **IV:** phone use before bed (yes vs. no)

- **DV:** sleep quality rating (1 = poor, 10 = excellent)

- **Design:** between-subjects, randomized

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Hypotheses

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Null hypothesis $H_0$

Sleep quality is the same with and without bedtime phone use.

$\mu_\text{no phone} = \mu_\text{phone}$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-important
## Alternative hypothesis $H_A$

Sleep quality differs between the conditions.

$\mu_\text{no phone} \neq \mu_\text{phone}$
:::
:::
:::::

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Data and results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.2
group_plot(sleep, "group", "sleep_quality", "Sleep quality (1-10)",
           "Phone use and sleep quality", kind = "bar")
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
results_tbl(sl)
```

No phone: $M = `r f2(sl$m1)`$, $SD = `r f2(sl$s1)`$. Phone: $M = `r f2(sl$m2)`$, $SD = `r f2(sl$s2)`$.
:::
:::::

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Run the test

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
sleep.R

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
t.test(sleep_quality ~ group, data = sleep, var.equal = TRUE)
```
:::

## Does bedtime phone use affect sleep?

### Decision, effect size, and report

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: callout-tip
## Decide

$t(`r sl$df`) = `r f2(sl$t)`$, $p$ `r fp(sl$p)`. Since $p > .05$, we **fail to reject** $H_0$. The result is close, but not significant.
:::

::: callout-tip
## Effect size

$d = \dfrac{`r f2(sl$diff)`}{`r f2(sl$sp)`} = `r f2(sl$d)`$ (a **small-to-medium** effect)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
> An independent-samples t-test showed that students who avoided their phones before bed (*M* = `r f2(sl$m1)`, *SD* = `r f2(sl$s1)`) did not differ significantly in sleep quality from students who used their phones (*M* = `r f2(sl$m2)`, *SD* = `r f2(sl$s2)`), [*`r apa_t(sl)`*]{.hl}, 95% CI [`r f2(sl$ci[1])`, `r f2(sl$ci[2])`], *d* = `r f2(sl$d)`.
:::
:::::

## Practice

### Caffeine and alertness

> Does caffeine increase alertness? 40 participants were randomly assigned to caffeine or a placebo (`ex_3`: `Group`, `Alertness`; 20 per group). Alertness was scored on a 0-100 scale.

::: {.callout-tip .nonincremental}
## Your tasks

1.  State $H_0$ and $H_A$.
2.  Check the equal-variance assumption (Levene's Test).
3.  Run the independent-samples t-test, compute $d$, and write an APA sentence.
:::

## Practice

### Caffeine and alertness: data and answer

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
practice_3.R

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
set.seed(103)
ex_3 <- tibble(
  Group = factor(rep(c("Caffeine", "Placebo"), each = 20),
                 levels = c("Caffeine", "Placebo")),
  Alertness = c(rnorm(20, mean = 75, sd = 8), rnorm(20, mean = 68, sd = 8))
)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-important .nonincremental}
## Answer

$H_0: \mu_\text{caffeine} = \mu_\text{placebo}$; $H_A: \mu_\text{caffeine} \neq \mu_\text{placebo}$. Caffeine $M = `r f2(e3$m1)`$ vs. placebo $M = `r f2(e3$m2)`$: *`r apa_t(e3)`*, 95% CI [`r f2(e3$ci[1])`, `r f2(e3$ci[2])`], $d = `r f2(e3$d)`$.
:::
:::

> Do exam scores differ between online and in-person sections? 25 students in each format took the same exam (`ex_4`: `Format`, `Exam_Score`).

::: {.callout-tip .nonincremental}

## Practice

### Online vs. in-person exams: data and answer

::: {.codewindow .r .codewindow-dark}
practice_4.R

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
#| eval: false
set.seed(104)
ex_4 <- tibble(
  Format = factor(rep(c("Online", "InPerson"), each = 25),
                  levels = c("Online", "InPerson")),
  Exam_Score = c(rnorm(25, mean = 82, sd = 5), rnorm(25, mean = 79, sd = 6))
)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-important .nonincremental}
## Answer

$H_0: \mu_\text{online} = \mu_\text{in-person}$; $H_A: \mu_\text{online} \neq \mu_\text{in-person}$. Online $M = `r f2(e4$m1)`$ vs. in-person $M = `r f2(e4$m2)`$: *`r apa_t(e4)`*, $d = `r f2(e4$d)`$. Compare $p$ to $\alpha = .05$ and interpret both the decision and the effect size.
:::
:::

## Summary: Independent-Samples t-Test

- Compares **two independent groups**.

- Tests whether the difference in means is significant.

- Uses **pooled variance** as the denominator when variances are equal (**Welch** when they are not).

- Check assumptions: independence, normality, equal variance (Levene's Test).

- Report the test, the means and SDs, the confidence interval, and an **effect size** ($d$).
